editorial_reason: Read Stacks 10.96, including its opening inverse-limit constructions and Definition 10.96.2. It specifies both ring and module completions for an ideal I and the canonical comparison defining I-adic completeness, which are genuinely different objects/properties.

definitions.text: For a commutative ring R and ideal I, its I-adic completion R^ is the inverse limit of the quotient rings R/I^n over positive integers n, with transition maps given by reduction modulo smaller powers.
definitions.context_hint: Commutative algebra: I-adic completion of a ring

definitions.text: For an R-module M and ideal I⊆R, the I-adic completion of M is lim_n M/I^n M; its elements can be viewed as mutually compatible residue classes modulo powers of I.
definitions.context_hint: Commutative algebra: I-adic completion of a module

definitions.text: An R-module M is I-adically complete when its canonical map M→lim_n M/I^n M is an isomorphism; a ring R is I-adically complete when it has this property as its own module.
definitions.context_hint: Commutative algebra: I-adically complete module or ring

editorial_reason: Read Stacks 10.23 'Glueing properties', whose lemmas establish local-to-global criteria for vanishing, exactness, and module maps across standard open coverings. The heading describes a collection of gluing theorems, not a newly defined object with a standalone definition in this chapter.

Read Stacks 10.99, particularly Lemma 10.99.7 (local criterion for flatness) and Lemma 10.99.10 (variant). The section gives a nontrivial precise equivalent test for flatness of a finite S-module over a Noetherian local base ring, not a new concept of flatness.

definitions.text: For a local map of Noetherian local rings R→S with residue field k of R and a finitely generated S-module M, M is flat over R if and only if Tor_1^R(k,M)=0.
definitions.context_hint: Commutative algebra: Tor-based local criterion for module flatness

editorial_reason: Read Stacks 9.3, Examples 9.3.1–9.3.3. They identify the rational field, the characteristic-p prime fields, and quotient constructions k[x]/(f) for irreducible polynomials. They are presented as examples rather than a uniform new field notion.

definitions.text: For a prime integer p, the finite prime field F_p is the quotient field Z/(p), whose elements are integer residue classes modulo p with operations inherited from integers.
definitions.context_hint: Field theory: finite prime field of characteristic p

definitions.text: For a field k and irreducible polynomial f in k[x], the quotient k[x]/(f) is a field extending k, obtained by adjoining the class of x as a root of f.
definitions.context_hint: Field theory: quotient field construction from an irreducible polynomial

editorial_reason: Read Stacks 10.60, Definitions 10.60.1, 10.60.2, 10.60.3 and 10.60.10. The source separates length of a chain of prime ideals, ring Krull dimension, prime ideal height, and parameters of a local ring.

definitions.text: A chain of prime ideals of R is a strictly increasing finite sequence p_0⊊p_1⊊⋯⊊p_n; its length is the number n of strict inclusions.
definitions.context_hint: Commutative algebra: chain and length of prime ideals

definitions.text: The Krull dimension of a commutative ring R is the supremum of the lengths of all finite strict chains of prime ideals in R, with the value infinite when those lengths are unbounded.
definitions.context_hint: Commutative algebra: Krull dimension of a ring

definitions.text: For a prime ideal p of a commutative ring R, the height of p is the Krull dimension of the local ring R_p, equivalently the supremum of lengths of strict prime chains terminating at p.
definitions.context_hint: Commutative algebra: height of a prime ideal

definitions.text: A system of parameters of a Noetherian local ring (R,m) of dimension d is a sequence of d elements of m whose generated ideal is m-primary, also called an ideal of definition.
definitions.context_hint: Commutative algebra: system of parameters of a Noetherian local ring

editorial_reason: Read Stacks 26.13, including its initial definition of h_X and Lemma 26.13.1 classifying maps from spectra of local rings. The source describes the functor of points and T-valued points, not merely topological points.

definitions.text: For a scheme X, its functor of points is the contravariant functor h_X from schemes to sets that assigns to a scheme T the set Hom_Sch(T,X), with pullback along T'→T defined by precomposition.
definitions.context_hint: Algebraic geometry: functor of points of a scheme

definitions.text: A T-valued point of a scheme X is a scheme morphism T→X; for T=Spec(k) with k a field, such a point is a map from the spectrum of k into X.
definitions.context_hint: Algebraic geometry: T-valued point of a scheme

editorial_reason: Read Stacks 10.61, 'Applications of dimension theory'. Its content applies previously defined Krull dimension and prime-ideal notions to prove infinitude and Jacobson-ring results; no independent mathematical object named 'applications of dimension theory' is defined in this section.

Read Stacks 9.21, Definitions 9.21.1 and 9.21.3, plus Lemma 9.21.2 giving the finite-degree automorphism characterization. The source explicitly defines Galois extension and associated Galois group as related but distinct objects.

definitions.text: A field extension E/F is Galois if it is algebraic, separable, and normal over F; for finite extensions this is equivalent to having precisely [E:F] F-automorphisms.
For a Galois extension E/F, the Galois group Gal(E/F) is the group of all field automorphisms of E that fix each element of F, with group law given by composition.
definitions.context_hint: Field theory: Galois group of an extension

editorial_reason: Read Stacks 10.95 on faithfully flat descent of properties of modules. Lemma 10.95.1 treats the Mittag-Leffler property and subsequent results treat projectivity under faithfully flat change, but the heading names applications of descent rather than a formally defined new mathematical object.

Read Stacks 10.114, 'Dimension of finite type algebras over fields'. It proves dimension computations for polynomial rings, finite-type algebras and regular localizations using previously defined dimension. No separate named notion of 'dimension of finite-type algebras' is introduced here.

Read Stacks 10.57, opening definition of a homogeneous ideal and Definition 10.57.1 of Proj(S), together with the degree-zero localization construction immediately afterward. These are related but different graded-ring constructions.

definitions.text: For a graded ring S=⊕_d S_d, an ideal I is homogeneous if it is graded as an S-submodule; equivalently, every homogeneous component of every element of I also belongs to I.

For a nonnegatively graded commutative ring S, Proj(S) is the topological space of homogeneous prime ideals that do not contain the irrelevant ideal S_+=⊕_{n>0}S_n, equipped with the subspace topology inherited from Spec(S).
definitions.context_hint: Graded commutative algebra: homogeneous spectrum Proj(S)

definitions.text: For a positively graded ring S and homogeneous element f of positive degree, S_(f) denotes the degree-zero subring of the graded localization S_f, consisting of fractions a/f^n with deg(a)=n·deg(f).
definitions.context_hint: Graded commutative algebra: degree-zero homogeneous localization

editorial_reason: Read Stacks 10.144, Definition 10.144.1 and Lemma 10.144.2. The defining conditions on a monic polynomial and its derivative give the notion of standard étale ring map; it is more specific than an arbitrary étale morphism.

definitions.text: A ring map R→S is standard étale when S is isomorphic as an R-algebra to R[x]_g/(f) for a monic polynomial f∈R[x] and polynomial g∈R[x], with f′ invertible in R[x]_g/(f).
definitions.context_hint: Commutative algebra: standard étale ring homomorphism
